chunks: Surface-mount vs through-hole. The question: What is the difference between surface-mount and through-hole components? Any tradeoffs?
Parts reach a board in two basic ways. Through-hole parts have wire legs that pass through drilled holes and are soldered on the other side.
Surface-mount parts sit flat on pads and are soldered on the same side. Surface-mount is smaller, cheaper at volume and better at high frequency.
Through-hole is stronger against pulling and bending.
Think of two ways to fix something to a wall. A sticker lies flat, goes on fast, and takes almost no room.
A nail goes right through and holds much harder when someone yanks on it. Small electronic parts are fine as stickers. A plug that people shove and pull needs the nail.
The analogy has one limit: the wire legs of a through-hole part also add electrical side effects, which a sticker-style part mostly avoids.
Magnitude of an ideal series-LC model (no ESR) of the same 100 nanofarads capacitor with different parasitic inductance.
Below the self-resonant frequency it behaves as a capacitor; above it, as an inductor, and the longer leads (red) lose their usefulness at a much lower frequency.
Real parts have ESR, which fills the notch.
Surface-mount (SMT): parts soldered flat onto pads on the board surface. Through-hole (THT): parts with legs that go through holes in the board.
Pad: the exposed copper patch where a part is soldered. Lead: the metal leg or terminal of a part. Inductance: a wire's resistance to fast changes in current.
A longer wire has more, and it matters at high frequency.
Decoupling capacitor: a small capacitor (a part that stores a little charge) placed next to a chip to supply quick bursts of current.
A straight 10 mm lead has about 7 nanohenries of inductance, and a small surface-mount capacitor has about 1 nanohenries.
At 100 megahertz, 7 nanohenries opposes current by about 4. 4 ohms, while 1 nanohenries opposes it by only about 0. 6 ohms.
So a decoupling capacitor on long legs helps much less at high frequency.
But a connector that gets plugged and unplugged all day is better held by through-hole legs, because small surface pads can tear off. That is the whole idea.
"Through-hole parts have leads that go through the board and are soldered on the back; surface-mount parts sit on pads on the surface and are reflow soldered.
SMT is smaller, denser, cheaper at volume because it's fully automated, and better at high frequency because it has almost no lead inductance.
Through-hole is mechanically stronger and easier to prototype and rework, so I'd still use it for connectors, large power parts and anything under mechanical stress.
A modern board is mostly SMT with a few through-hole parts."
